subtype: Reverence and respect in shared spaces [Expressing]
passage:
Dear Zainab,

On Friday our school visited the gurdwara, and I was nervous because I wasn't sure what to do. I didn't want to be disrespectful. So I watched the others: they took off their shoes and washed their hands and feet, and covered their heads. The volunteer at the door noticed me looking around and handed me a clean scarf with a smile. I tied it on. Inside, everyone sat on the floor and the music was so calm that even the noisy boys went quiet. Afterwards I asked a woman there why people bow, and she explained gladly. You'd like it, I think.

Love,
Rehana 🙂

qa.q: What did the volunteer at the door hand Rehana?
qa.a: The volunteer handed Rehana a clean scarf.

qa.q: Why did Rehana watch the others before acting?
qa.a: Rehana was nervous and did not want to be disrespectful, so watched what people did and copied respectfully. Rehana was uncertain, not careless.

qa.q: What would you advise a visitor who is unsure of the customs somewhere?
qa.a: Watch what others do, follow it respectfully and ask politely if unsure, as Rehana did.

qa.q: How might the volunteer have felt seeing Rehana look around?
qa.a: The volunteer may have felt welcoming and happy to help, having offered the scarf with a smile. 🙂

grounding: A teen shows respect in a gurdwara by watching others and politely asking, noting practices differ.

passage: So Mridul, you know how I was dreading the temple trip in Madurai? I'd never been inside one with all those carvings and people. At the entrance my cousin whispered, 'Shoes here.' So I left mine on the rack with everyone's, and I felt the cool stone under my feet. I kept my voice low. People stood with folded hands, and I stood a bit back, not sure where to stand. An old man saw me hesitating and said, 'Come, you can stand here, it's fine.' I thanked him. Nobody made me do anything. I just watched, asked once, and it felt like being a guest instead of a tourist. Eshaan, signing off.

qa.q: Where was the temple trip?
qa.a: The temple trip was in Madurai.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan stand back and keep a low voice inside the temple?
qa.a: Eshaan was not sure where to stand and wanted to be respectful as a visitor. The hesitation shows uncertainty rather than lack of interest.

qa.q: What could Eshaan do on a future visit to an unfamiliar place of worship?
qa.a: Watch what others do, follow along politely and ask if unsure, as Eshaan did with the old man.

qa.q: How might the old man have felt seeing Eshaan hesitate?
qa.a: He probably felt kind and welcoming, wanting the visitor to feel comfortable. 🙂

grounding: A teen shows reverence in a temple by removing shoes and being quiet and asking politely, noting practices differ.

passage:
I'm Ishita, and I took my friend Aadhya to the gurdwara near our school for the first time on Sunday. I noticed everything she did because I was nervous for her.
At the entrance she stopped and watched. People were taking off shoes and leaving them at the counter. She did the same. Then she saw that everyone had their heads covered, and she pulled her dupatta up before I could say anything.
Inside, she sat on the floor next to me and was very quiet. When everyone stood, she stood too, a second late.
At the langar hall she whispered to the sevadar, "Sorry, is it okay if I sit anywhere?" He smiled and said, "Sit, beta, anywhere."
Afterwards Aadhya said, "I was scared I'd do something wrong." I don't know if she enjoyed it. But she asked to come again.

qa.q: What did Aadhya pull up before Ishita could say anything?
qa.a: She pulled her dupatta up to cover her head.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling during her first visit?
qa.a: Aadhya was nervous and careful, scared of doing something wrong, which is why she watched others closely.

qa.q: What made Aadhya's visit go well?
qa.a: She watched what others did, copied the respectful practices, and asked the sevadar politely when unsure.

qa.q: How might the sevadar have seen Aadhya's question?
qa.a: He seemed to see it as a sign of respect and welcomed her warmly, calling her beta.

grounding: A friend's account shows a first-time visitor showing respect in a gurdwara by watching others and politely asking.

passage:
Friday: Deepak had never been inside a church. His friend Arohi's cousin was getting married on Saturday. At lunch he asked her, "What should I do? I don't want to get anything wrong." Arohi laughed. "Just watch me. Stand when we stand. Sit when we sit. Be quiet when it's quiet."
Saturday: In the church, the air smelled of candles and flowers. Deepak kept his phone in his pocket and his eyes on Arohi. When people knelt, he wasn't sure, so he stayed seated with his head bowed, and nobody seemed to mind. During the vows the church was so silent he could hear the fans.
Monday: Deepak told Arohi, "The quiet part during the vows. I didn't expect that to feel so big."
"You were very respectful," she said. "My aunt noticed."
He smiled, a little embarrassed.

qa.q: When was the wedding?
qa.a: The wedding was on Saturday.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling at lunch on Friday?
qa.a: Deepak was nervous and unsure, worried he might get something wrong in an unfamiliar place.

qa.q: How did Deepak show respect when he wasn't sure what to do?
qa.a: He watched Arohi, kept his phone away, and when unsure about kneeling, stayed seated with his head bowed.

qa.q: How might Arohi's aunt have seen Deepak?
qa.a: She seemed to notice and appreciate his respectful, quiet behaviour as a guest from a different faith.

grounding: The three beats show a teenager asking and watching others to show reverence in a church he had never visited.

passage:
Gurpreet, you're worried about the school trip to the mosque tomorrow? Let your Jyoti Dadi tell you what happened to me.
At fifteen, my school took us to the old mosque in our city. I was so busy looking at the arches that I walked straight onto the prayer carpet with my sandals on.
An old man sweeping the courtyard called out, "Beti!" I thought he'd shout. Instead he pointed gently at my feet, then at the row of shoes by the steps. I went red and ran back.
He wasn't angry at all. He showed me where to wash my hands and told me where I could sit and watch quietly. When I asked about the carvings, he explained for ten minutes.
So tomorrow, watch what others do first. And if you don't know, ask politely. Most people are happy you asked.

qa.q: What did Jyoti walk onto with her sandals on?
qa.a: She walked straight onto the prayer carpet with her sandals on.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel when the old man called out?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and scared, going red and expecting to be shouted at.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Jyoti Dadi's story?
qa.a: The old man gently pointing at her feet instead of shouting, which let her correct the mistake and then ask about the carvings.

qa.q: How might the old man have seen the young visitor?
qa.a: He probably saw an honest mistake by a curious girl, which is why he corrected her gently and happily answered her questions.

grounding: The elder's story shows a visitor learning to show respect in a mosque by watching others and politely asking.

passage: The rain came down so hard on the school heritage walk that the group scattered, and Gautam and Tanuja ended up alone at the gate of the old gurdwara, soaked and without their teacher. "Can we just wait inside?" Tanuja whispered. Gautam hesitated at the steps. Everyone around them was slipping off their shoes into the racks and rinsing their feet in a shallow channel of water. He copied them, then noticed every head was covered, even a toddler's. He had nothing. He went up to an older man handing out tea and asked quietly, "Sorry, uncle, I'm visiting. Is it okay to come in, and do I need to cover my head?" The man smiled and pulled two orange cloths from a basket. "Both of you. Welcome." Inside, the hymns were soft and steady. Gautam sat cross-legged near the back, dripping, and didn't take out his phone once. When the teacher's call finally came, he stepped outside before answering.

qa.q: What did the older man pull from the basket?
qa.a: He pulled two orange cloths from a basket.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling as he hesitated at the steps?
qa.a: Gautam felt unsure and a bit nervous about getting unfamiliar customs wrong, while wanting to be respectful; it might also have been shyness about being soaked and alone.

qa.q: How did Gautam work out what to do?
qa.a: He watched the people around him and copied the shoes and foot rinsing, then asked politely about covering his head instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might the older man have seen the two soaked visitors?
qa.a: The man seemed glad they asked, smiling and handing both of them cloths, so he likely saw them as respectful guests.

grounding: It shows a teenager showing respect in an unfamiliar place of worship by removing shoes, covering the head and staying quiet, learning by watching and politely asking.
